CO1: Describe the Bitcoin network as a flat peer-to-peer network of equal nodes, name the services nodes differ in, and read what a census of reachable nodes shows
CO2: Follow how a node joins: DNS seeds, the version handshake and its services, address exchange, and the kinds of connection a node keeps
CO3: Explain how a block travels (announcement, compact blocks, private relay) and how a node syncs headers first and blocks after, and judge why speed matters for rival blocks
CO4: Compare a light client that checks headers and Merkle paths, the Bloom filters of BIP 37 that leaked privacy, and the block filters of BIPs 157 and 158 that replaced them
CO5: Explain what the encrypted v2 transport and the Tor, I2P and CJDNS networks hide, and judge the eclipse and routing attacks on the network
CO6: Explain how transactions are announced and filtered, why every mempool is local, and what a node does with a child that arrives before its parent
_serves: These six outcomes are chapter 10's: the network and its nodes (CO1), joining it (CO2), moving blocks (CO3, with syncing), light clients (CO4), privacy and attacks (CO5) and the mempool with orphans (CO6). The chapter serves LO-6 of the course (reading and constructing transactions, scripts and signatures and explaining how a node decides whether one is valid). Each outcome is worded with one level of Bloom's taxonomy (Understand, Apply, Analyze or Evaluate here). Written by the page author from the chapter's own subjects; the research states no learning outcomes of its own.
